Experiments cover four long-horizon domains, including manipulation and navigation, four dataset-quality levels, held-out tasks, and five random seeds. PRISM's improvements over SPiRL and SiMPL are generally large and consistent, especially at severe noise levels.
The component, temperature, and exploration-regularization ablations are useful, while learning curves and qualitative skill visualizations provide more evidence than final-return tables alone.
The appendix gives extensive environment, architecture, and hyperparameter information, and the adaptive use of offline and newly collected trajectories is intuitively well motivated.
weaknesses: The comparison does not establish equal interaction or compute budgets. PRISM collects both high-level-policy and exploration-policy trajectories for every training task and performs additional skill and reward-model updates, whereas SiMPL and SPiRL lack this second data stream. Reporting results against an ambiguously defined “iteration,” without total environment steps, episodes, gradient updates, or runtime, leaves open whether the gains primarily result from substantially more clean online data and computation.

There is no decisive equal-budget baseline that gives SiMPL/SPiRL the same online trajectories and permits ordinary low-level skill fine-tuning. SAC+RND and PEARL+RND do not control for this because they lack the hierarchical skill architecture. The existing ablations therefore do not cleanly attribute improvements to maximum-return relabeling rather than generic offline-to-online refinement.

Important algorithmic definitions are internally inconsistent. The task-specific online buffer is said to be initialized with the reward-free offline dataset, yet insertion thresholds, its average return, and reward-model training all assume true rewards for its contents; its stated 10K capacity also conflicts with initializing it from datasets containing 0.5–1M transitions. Priority initialization and handling of the unscored or stale offline trajectories are unspecified.

The mathematical presentation raises further soundness and reproducibility concerns: the exploration critic target in Eq. A.3 uses Q plus the positive entropy coefficient times log-policy, opposite to the standard SAC target sign implied by the actor loss; Eq. A.6 uses the state at t+Hs-1 after an Hs-action skill, inconsistent with the t+Hs state used earlier; and the entropy coefficient is described as both automatically adjusted and fixed in the hyperparameter table.

The central learned prioritizer is insufficiently validated. There is no measurement of reward-model accuracy or ranking quality, no comparison with oracle-return priorities, and no ablation of maximum-over-tasks aggregation against alternatives. Taking a maximum over many task-conditioned reward predictions can amplify out-of-distribution overestimation, while the “without PBoff” ablation may still use predicted returns through the mixing coefficient beta.

The robustness evidence is narrow: every corruption is fixed-variance i.i.d. Gaussian action noise applied to oracle policies in simulation. Mixed-quality demonstrations, temporally correlated or biased noise, observation noise, human data, and real-robot perturbations are absent, so the broad real-world robustness claims are not supported.

Hyperparameters are selected using the best reported task performance, with the exploration regularizer even chosen separately for each Kitchen noise level, but no validation-task protocol is described. This creates a material test-selection risk, and baseline tuning is not documented comparably.

The contribution is largely a composition of established mechanisms—RND, elite replay, learned reward relabeling, softmax prioritization, and SPiRL/SiMPL—and is not compared with robust demonstration-learning or denoising approaches. Missing code links and omitted rollout/pretraining/update counts further limit reproducibility. Overall, the promising results do not overcome the evaluation-control and specification gaps required for acceptance at a top-tier venue.

strengths: The paper targets an important, practically motivated weakness of skill-based meta-RL: degradation when demonstrations are noisy or suboptimal. The proposed combination of online exploration, return-based relabeling, and prioritized skill refinement is intuitive.

The evaluation includes useful component ablations, hyperparameter sensitivity studies, learning curves, and qualitative visualizations of skill refinement.
The appendix documents task splits, dataset construction, model architectures, and many hyperparameters, and provides pseudocode and expanded objectives.
weaknesses: The central comparison is not demonstrably sample- or compute-matched. Each PRISM iteration collects both high-level-policy and separate exploration-policy trajectories, whereas the main baselines generally use one collection stream. Results are plotted against vaguely defined iterations rather than environment interactions, so the improvements may partly reflect substantially more online data. A sample-matched SiMPL variant with online skill fine-tuning and simpler replay/filtering controls is essential.

Hyperparameter selection risks test leakage. The paper selects the best exploration KL coefficient separately for each noise level, and the supporting sweeps report meta-test return; no validation tasks, seeds, or selection protocol are described. Baseline tuning is also much less clearly specified.

There are consequential technical ambiguities and inconsistencies. The online buffer is said to be initialized with reward-free offline data, yet insertion thresholds, reward-model training, and the control factor require actual returns from that buffer. Equation A.3 uses the opposite sign from the standard SAC entropy term in the critic target, and several high-level transitions use s_(t+Hs-1) where s_(t+Hs) appears required. It is unclear whether these are presentation errors or reflect the implementation.

Maximum return relabeling applies a maximum over task-conditioned reward-model predictions on offline trajectories that may be out of distribution. This invites extrapolation and maximization bias, but the paper provides no reward-model accuracy, calibration, ranking-quality, or oracle-reward comparison.

The robustness evidence is narrow: all corruption is synthetic i.i.d. Gaussian action noise added to oracle policies. There are no experiments with human demonstrations, mixed-quality trajectories, structured or adversarial errors, observation noise, or dynamics mismatch, so claims about general noisy real-world data are substantially broader than the evidence.

Novelty is moderate because the method largely composes SiMPL/SPiRL, SAC, RND, reward prediction, prioritized replay, and periodic retraining. Comparisons to robust imitation methods cited by the paper, straightforward online retraining, or other data-reweighting approaches are absent.

Reproducibility is inadequate despite the detailed appendix: all promised repository URLs are blank, and important quantities such as environment steps, rollout counts, gradient steps, target-network handling, priority initialization, and total compute are unspecified. The paper's claim of comparable computation per iteration does not resolve these omissions.

The method still requires extensive rewarded online interaction during both meta-training and 500 adaptation iterations per test task. This weakens the framing of robustness to offline demonstrations and the claim of rapid, real-world adaptation; safety implications of exploratory robot interaction are not discussed.

SISL adds a primitive-action, task-conditioned improvement policy, online environment rewards, extra rollout collection, and continual low-level retraining. The paper reports iterations and per-iteration runtime, but not matched environment steps or trajectories. Consequently, the gains may partly reflect substantially more online experience and model capacity rather than robustness to demonstrations.

Crucial matched baselines are missing: SiMPL with the same online interaction budget and continual skill fine-tuning, SiMPL/SPiRL with RND or elite replay, simple learned-return filtering, and an oracle-return prioritization variant. The dismissal of offline-to-online methods because the demonstrations lack rewards is also incomplete, since SISL itself learns an online reward model for relabeling.

The reward-based prioritization mechanism is insufficiently validated. The reported reward-model MSE is not identified as held-out error and does not test predictions on the offline trajectories, which are precisely the out-of-distribution samples being ranked. Taking the maximum prediction across task models can amplify optimistic errors, while beta compares predicted offline returns with actual online returns. No ranking accuracy, calibration, or oracle-reward ablation is provided.

The algorithm description contains a consequential contradiction: Section 4 says each prioritized online buffer is initialized with the reward-free offline dataset, whereas Appendix F.4 says these buffers contain only online trajectories. If reward-free samples are included, the minimum-return replacement rule and mean online return are undefined without additional relabeling. Empty-buffer initialization, per-task handling, and the replay-buffer reset mentioned only in a later ablation are also underspecified.

Hyperparameter selection appears asymmetric. SISL-specific parameters are swept, and the KL coefficient is selected separately for individual Kitchen noise levels, while baseline tuning budgets are not reported. This uses knowledge of the corruption condition and may materially favor SISL.

Most corruptions are synthetic Gaussian action noise. Random-action injection, reduced data, and suboptimal-data tests are confined to Kitchen, and the so-called diverse-quality experiment evaluates separate homogeneous expert, medium, and random datasets rather than a heterogeneous mixture. There is no observation noise, dynamics corruption, real noisy demonstration dataset, or hardware experiment, so claims about real-world robustness are too strong.

The contribution is primarily a combination of established ingredients—SAC, RND, behavioral cloning toward elite trajectories, prioritized replay, and periodic skill retraining. Its novelty relative to robust imitation learning, online skill discovery, and offline-to-online RL is not established through sufficiently direct comparisons.

Several technical and reproducibility details remain unclear, including exact environment-step and gradient-update counts, target/twin critics in the SAC implementation, and the apparent entropy-sign convention in the critic target. Five seeds without confidence intervals or significance testing are also weak support for the smaller clean-data improvements.

strengths: Addresses an important and underexplored problem: robust skill-based meta-RL when reward-free demonstrations are noisy or suboptimal.
The proposed combination of online skill refinement, high-return buffering, and reward-model-based trajectory prioritization is intuitively motivated and technically plausible.

The empirical study is broad, covering four long-horizon domains, multiple Gaussian-noise levels, random-action corruption, reduced dataset sizes, and different dataset qualities, generally with substantial gains over SPiRL and SiMPL.
Five-seed results, component ablations, hyperparameter studies, computational measurements, detailed task definitions, and extensive implementation information are useful reproducibility efforts.
weaknesses: The comparison does not establish matched online interaction budgets. Each SISL iteration collects trajectories from both the high-level and improvement policies and additionally retrains the skill model, while the baselines apparently do not receive equivalent interactions. The ambiguous iteration accounting and per-iteration timing comparison do not rule out extra online data or optimization as the main source of improvement.

Hyperparameter selection risks test leakage. The paper presents sweeps using meta-test returns and then selects the best settings, including different KL coefficients for individual Kitchen noise levels, without specifying validation tasks or a selection protocol independent of the reported test set. This also assumes knowledge of the corruption level and gives SISL substantially more condition-specific tuning than is documented for the baselines.

The most informative matched baselines are missing: SiMPL or SPiRL with online skill fine-tuning, RND, high-return replay, or an equivalent interaction budget, as well as applicable robust imitation/noisy-demonstration methods. Component ablations do not fully substitute for these comparisons and are reported comprehensively for only two environments.

The algorithm description contains consequential inconsistencies. The main text says the task-specific online buffer is initialized with the reward-free offline dataset, whereas the appendix defines it as containing online trajectories and the pseudocode does not initialize it; filtering against the minimum return of an initially empty buffer is undefined. Moreover, the claimed constraint keeping the improvement policy near the offline manifold is only a behavioral-cloning term to the online buffer. The scope of high-level reinitialization is also inconsistent across the text, pseudocode, and ablation description.

The central reward-model relabeling mechanism is insufficiently validated. Reward models trained on visited online transitions are applied to potentially out-of-distribution offline trajectories, and maximizing predictions across tasks can amplify extrapolation error. The reported MSE on online buffers does not demonstrate accurate offline ranking, calibration, or correct prioritization. The mixing coefficient also compares differently constructed online and predicted-offline returns.

The robustness evidence is limited mainly to synthetic action corruption in simulation and tasks that recombine familiar subtasks or goals. It does not cover naturally noisy demonstrations, observation noise, dynamics shifts, or real robotic data, so the strong real-world robustness and generalization claims exceed the evidence.

Some ablation conclusions are overstated: removing prioritization or the improvement policy is neutral or even slightly beneficial in certain Maze2D conditions, and no statistical significance analysis is provided. More broadly, the contribution combines several established mechanisms—SAC, RND, top-return replay, behavior cloning, and periodic skill retraining—without theory or sufficiently controlled experiments isolating novelty from additional training resources.
